title: Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification

paper.title: Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification
paper.abstract: Abstract We revisit the influential distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022), whose optimal disclosure policy reveals low bidder values and pools high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders, and show that this policy is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once bidders can endogenously acquire private information through costly verification. The underlying reason reflects a fundamental principle of incentive-based mechanism design, rooted in Hurwicz’s analysis of structural invariance and echoed in the Lucas critique: economic agents respond strategically to changes in the information and incentives they face. This is the essence of trust, but verify . A change in disclosure policy may leave the underlying economic primitives unchanged while altering bidders’ verification decisions and the resulting equilibrium information structure. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium, characterize equilibrium-implementable disclosure policies, and derive an exact revenue decomposition and a general characterization of global optimality. We further develop optimality conditions and structural results that provide a systematic foundation for analyzing optimal disclosure with endogenous information acquisition.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: How much information should a seller disclose to bidders in an auction? Providing more information can help bidders determine what an object is worth to them and improve the allocation of the object. But better-informed bidders may also obtain greater information rents, reducing the seller’s revenue. Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022, henceforth BHMSW) study this trade-off in a classic second-price auction in which bidders initially do not know their own valuations and the seller chooses what information they receive. They establish a striking result: the revenue-maximizing disclosure policy fully reveals low values while pooling high values. Under this low-value-revelation/high-value-pooling policy, the cutoff is determined by the number of bidders in quantile space, independently of the underlying distribution of valuations. Although developed for second-price auctions, BHMSW explain that their benchmark result also applies to classical revenue-equivalent auction formats, including first-price and all-pay auctions, under the relevant independent private-value assumptions. The strength of this result lies in its simple disclosure structure and distribution-independent critical quantile. It is therefore natural to ask whether the same policy remains optimal when the bidders themselves can respond to the seller’s disclosure by producing information. This is not a change in the auction’s allocation rule or in the prior distribution of values. It is a change in what bidders can do after receiving the information the seller chooses to provide. As we show, that additional margin is enough to overturn the generality of the benchmark disclosure conclusion. In many auctions, however, bidders do not rely exclusively on information supplied by the seller. Consider auctions of valuable artworks, antiques, and other collectibles. Sellers provide descriptions and information about the objects offered for sale, but prospective buyers may also conduct their own investigations to determine what those objects are worth to them. Such behavior follows a familiar principle: trust, but verify. Even when the seller’s information is reliable, it need not be sufficient for a bidder to assess her own valuation. Further investigation can provide valuable information, but requires time, effort, or money. The bidder must decide whether obtaining that information is worth its cost. For a buyer considering a painting or an antique, the question is not simply whether to believe a catalogue entry. Information can be credible and still incomplete for deciding how much to bid. A buyer may examine provenance records, commission an independent appraisal, inspect the object, or seek evidence about authenticity and condition. Doing so takes resources; choosing not to do so leaves the buyer exposed to uncertainty. The familiar injunction to “trust, but verify” therefore has a direct strategic meaning in an auction: what a bidder learns privately depends on the information already disclosed, the cost of further investigation, and the bids she expects to face. This possibility changes the seller’s disclosure problem. Pooling high values may increase revenue by limiting the information rents bidders obtain from the seller’s disclosure. Yet the uncertainty left by pooling can also encourage bidders to acquire additional information privately. The seller therefore faces two related considerations: how disclosure directly affects competition and revenue, and how it changes bidders’ incentives to verify their values. Each bidder faces a corresponding trade-off between the expected benefit of making a better-informed bidding decision and the cost of verification. Moreover, the value of verification depends on how well informed competing bidders are. The seller’s disclosure policy and bidders’ information-acquisition decisions are consequently linked through equilibrium behavior. The principle of “trust, but verify” reflects a deeper lesson of incentive-based economic analysis: agents do not passively accept the information supplied by a designer, but respond to the incentives created by the designer’s policy. This observation echoes Hurwicz (1962) ’s fundamental insight that structural relationships must be understood relative to the changes under consideration, and the related concern underlying the Lucas (1976) critique that policy changes may alter agents’ behavioral decision rules. In the present setting, a change in disclosure policy leaves the underlying valuation environment and verification technology unchanged, but changes bidders’ incentives to acquire information and hence the equilibrium informational environment in which the auction operates. The seller cannot therefore evaluate alternative disclosure policies while treating bidders’ information-acquisition decisions as invariant. Information disclosure is not merely a choice of what information to reveal; it is also an intervention that changes the incentives to learn. This interaction has a central implication. The distribution-independent optimal disclosure result established by Bergemann et al. (2022)—revealing low values while pooling high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders—does not remain generally revenue maximizing when verification is an endogenous choice. We establish the failure of that recommendation in two of the most elementary and familiar valuation environments in auction theory: uniform and binary values. The significance of these findings is not that a specially tailored distribution creates an exception. Rather, the benchmark policy already loses its generality in settings that normally serve as the starting point for auction analysis. The original BHMSW theorem remains valid under its own assumptions; what does not survive is the extension of its optimal disclosure conclusion to a world in which bidders can privately verify their values. The economic reason is the seller’s interaction with bidders’ information production. Revealing information can improve bidding decisions while raising information rents; withholding it may limit those rents while inducing bidders to learn for themselves. A bidder, in turn, weighs the expected advantage of better information against the cost of verification, taking into account how informed her competitors are likely to become. Thus neither the seller’s disclosure choice nor a bidder’s verification choice can be assessed in isolation. The relevant object is the Bayesian Nash equilibrium induced by each disclosure policy, and the seller compares revenues across those equilibria. We study this interaction by extending the independent private-value environment of BHMSW. The seller continues to choose symmetric, independent private information experiments about bidders’ original valuations, and the object is sold through a second-price auction. After receiving the seller’s signal, however, each bidder may privately undertake costly verification to learn more about her own valuation. Verification is a hidden action, and its outcome provides additional private information without changing the underlying valuation. We focus on a simple information-production technology in which the bidder chooses an effort that determines the probability of learning her valuation perfectly. The seller anticipates the equilibrium verification decisions when choosing the initial information structure. The distinction between information disclosed by the seller and information acquired by bidders is important. In the original disclosure problem, the seller can choose the distribution of bidders’ posterior expected valuations, subject to Bayes plausibility. Once verification is possible, the same distribution of posterior means may induce different information-acquisition incentives. A bidder’s willingness to verify depends not only on her expected valuation but also on the uncertainty that remains about her actual value. Thus, the seller must take account of the full posterior beliefs generated by disclosure and the subsequent information choices of bidders. The failure of the benchmark policy also creates a constructive problem: if the seller cannot treat the final information in bidders’ hands as something she directly controls, how should optimal disclosure be characterized? Our analysis proceeds from the bidders’ Bayesian Nash equilibrium in private verification to the seller’s feasible equilibrium outcomes, and then to general revenue and optimality conditions. This positive theory complements the main economic finding rather than merely providing a way to calculate the examples. Our first contribution, developed in Section 3, is to characterize the equilibrium of this information-acquisition game. A bidder’s gain from verification depends on the distribution of competing bids, which in turn depends on their verification decisions. This strategic feedback leads to a fixed-point problem that must be resolved before evaluating the seller’s disclosure policy. We show that the symmetric verification equilibrium admits a convex-potential representation, which establishes existence and uniqueness under strictly convex verification costs. The associated equilibrium Jacobian has a positive-semidefinite Gram structure, providing a tractable characterization of equilibrium interactions and comparative statics. We extend the existence and uniqueness results from finite signal structures to arbitrary posterior distributions using fixed-point and potential arguments. The resulting equilibrium characterization also establishes continuity of the final-bid distribution with respect to the seller’s information experiment, a key step in proving the existence of an optimal disclosure policy over the unrestricted experiment space. Our second contribution, developed in Section 5, concerns optimal disclosure for general distributions of bidder values. We characterize which final-bid distributions can arise from a Bayes-plausible private disclosure experiment together with the bidders’ equilibrium verification choices. The characterization applies to the unrestricted space of private information experiments rather than a prespecified family of disclosure policies. Using convex separation and concavification, we obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for equilibrium implementability, together with a posterior-price dual representation. These results provide an infinite-dimensional characterization of feasible disclosure outcomes without requiring concavity of the seller’s revenue function or imposing a particular form on the optimal experiment. This general characterization addresses a difficulty created by endogenous information acquisition. Although the seller chooses the initial information structure, she does not directly choose the final distribution of bids. That distribution results from the combination of disclosure and bidders’ privately chosen verification efforts. Consequently, standard information-design arguments based only on distributions of posterior means are no longer sufficient. Our characterization identifies the additional equilibrium restrictions that a final-bid distribution must satisfy. It provides a general description of feasible disclosure outcomes without imposing a particular structure on the seller’s optimal experiment. In Sections 5 and 6, to study the structure of optimal disclosure more directly, we derive the revenue effects of changes in the seller’s information policy, allowing verification efforts to adjust in equilibrium. Using the implicit-function theorem, we separate the direct effect of disclosure on bidding from the indirect effect operating through endogenous verification. We also develop a rare-signal splitting test that introduces new private signals while preserving Bayes plausibility. The resulting directional condition accounts for both equilibrium effort adjustments and changes in the distribution of bids, including moving bid atoms. This provides a rigorous test of whether a proposed disclosure policy can be improved and plays a central role in establishing the failure of the benchmark disclosure structure. Our third contribution, established in Section 4, is a sharp result on that question. We first characterize verification equilibrium under the benchmark policy for general distributions of bidder values. In this case, bidders whose values are fully revealed have no reason to verify, while those receiving the pooled high-value signal face a nontrivial information-acquisition decision. The equilibrium therefore reduces to a one-dimensional problem. For three bidders with uniformly distributed valuations, we obtain closed-form expressions for verification effort and seller revenue, allowing us to study how endogenous verification changes the optimal pooling cutoff. The analysis in Section 4 shows that the benchmark disclosure conclusion of BHMSW does not generally survive endogenous information acquisition. Consider three bidders with independent uniform valuations and quadratic verification costs. We first identify the revenue-maximizing policy within the entire class of policies that reveal lower values and pool higher values. We then construct an admissible refinement of its high-value pool and account for the verification equilibrium induced by the refined information structure. The refinement yields strictly higher expected revenue than the optimal policy within that benchmark class. The comparison is established analytically by an exact polynomial root count and rational revenue bounds, rather than inferred from a numerical comparison of selected disclosure policies. The economic mechanism behind this result is the interaction between pooling and private verification. Pooling high values can benefit the seller when bidders do not acquire additional information. But the same pooling leaves uncertainty that bidders may find worthwhile to resolve. Refining the high-value pool changes not only what bidders initially know but also how much additional information they choose to acquire. The seller can therefore gain from a disclosure policy that would not be optimal if bidders’ information-acquisition decisions were held fixed. The failure of low-value revelation and high-value pooling arises from this equilibrium response, not from any change in the auction format or in bidders’ original valuation distributions. Our findings distinguish the value of partial disclosure from the particular structure of optimal partial disclosure. The result of BHMSW remains valid in their original environment, which is recovered when additional information acquisition is unavailable. In our extended environment, full disclosure need not be optimal either. What changes is the revenue-maximizing way of withholding and revealing information. The counterexample establishes that no policy in that benchmark class is optimal in the specified environment, although it does not identify an explicit optimal experiment over the unrestricted disclosure space. The general equilibrium and implementability results provide a framework for studying that broader problem. Our analysis relates to two strands of research. The first studies information disclosure and Bayesian persuasion, where a designer chooses an information structure to influence subsequent decisions. BHMSW apply this approach to classic auctions and establish the benchmark result that serves as our point of departure. The second studies endogenous information acquisition, including bidders’ incentives to learn before participating in auctions. Our contribution connects these approaches: the seller chooses an information structure while anticipating that bidders will respond by privately acquiring additional information. This interaction changes both the set of equilibrium bidding outcomes and the structure of the seller’s optimal disclosure policy.

sections.heading: Related Literature
sections.text: Our study draws most directly on two lines of research: the design of information disclosed by an auction seller and the costly acquisition of information by bidders. Bergemann et al. (2022) provide the central benchmark by identifying a revenue-maximizing rule that reveals lower values and pools higher values in a second-price auction. Their analysis highlights the tension between the allocative gains from informing bidders and the information rents that more precise private knowledge may create. Our question is what happens to that conclusion when the seller’s disclosure also changes bidders’ incentives to learn privately. The auction format and the distribution of underlying valuations are unchanged; the new margin is the endogenous information acquired after the seller’s signals. The two familiar valuation environments examined in Section 4 show why that margin matters for the robustness of the benchmark conclusion ( Bergemann et al., 2022 ) . The classical auction literature emphasizes the role of information in bidding and revenue. Milgrom and Weber (1982a) develop the foundational analysis of auctions with interdependent information and the consequences of information disclosure; Milgrom and Weber (1982b) study the value and strategic acquisition of information in sealed-bid auctions. Bergemann and Pesendorfer (2007) analyze the joint choice of an optimal auction and bidders’ information structures. These approaches provide essential antecedents for studying information as an economic design margin. Our question is narrower in auction format but different in equilibrium timing: the second-price auction is fixed, and seller disclosure precedes bidders’ privately chosen costly verification ( Milgrom and Weber, 1982a ; Milgrom and Weber, 1982b ; Bergemann and Pesendorfer, 2007 ) . A closely related literature studies strategic and costly information acquisition in auctions. Persico (2000) examines the incentives to acquire information under alternative auction mechanisms; Bobkova (2024) studies how auction formats shape the information about an object that bidders choose to learn. These contributions show why an information-acquisition decision is itself part of auction behavior rather than an exogenous input to bidding. We instead hold the second-price auction fixed and allow the seller to choose what bidders initially learn before their costly private verification decisions. This distinction is important: the verification decisions form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium and change the final distribution of bids through which the seller’s disclosure affects revenue ( Persico, 2000 ; Bobkova, 2024 ) . A further auction-theoretic connection concerns endogenous costly decisions before bidding. Bergemann and Välimäki (2002) study incentives for private information acquisition under mechanism design. In an earlier line of research, Cao and Tian (2010) analyze equilibrium participation decisions in first- and second-price auctions with participation costs; Cao et al. (2018) study related second-price environments, including privately known participation costs. These studies already feature the central economic insight that bidders compare the expected equilibrium benefit of a privately costly choice with its cost, taking other bidders’ choices into account. In the present paper, the costly choice concerns verification rather than entry, and the new design margin is the seller’s information disclosure, which endogenously changes the benefit of acquiring private information ( Bergemann and Välimäki, 2002 ; Cao and Tian, 2010 ; Cao et al., 2018 ) . Our approach also connects to the broader literature on statistical experiments and information design. Blackwell’s comparison of experiments provides a foundational language for informativeness; Bayesian persuasion and Bayes-correlated-equilibrium approaches emphasize the choice of informational structures and the resulting constraints on beliefs and behavior ( Blackwell, 1953 ; Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011 ; Bergemann and Morris, 2016 ; Bergemann and Morris, 2019 ) . Bergemann, Bonatti, and Smolin (2018) study information as an economic object that can itself be designed and priced. Joint mechanism–information design similarly underscores the importance of coordinating informational and incentive instruments ( Bergemann et al., 2018 ; Bergemann et al., 2026a ) . In the present setting, however, the seller does not directly choose the final information on which bids are based. Initial posterior beliefs determine verification incentives, and the equilibrium information acquired by bidders determines the eventual bidding distribution. Section 5 characterizes precisely this additional implementability restriction. The distinction between supplying information and inducing private learning also arises outside auctions. Crémer and Khalil (1992), Lewis and Sappington (1994), and Crémer, Khalil, and Rochet (1998) examine how contractual and informational arrangements affect incentives to become informed. These studies help distinguish information already held by agents from information they choose to acquire after observing an institutional decision. The present paper carries this interaction into a seller’s optimal disclosure problem with competing bidders and equilibrium verification ( Crémer and Khalil, 1992 ; Lewis and Sappington, 1994 ; Crémer et al., 1998 ) . A further connection is to endogenous information production and dynamic mechanism design. Research on experimentation emphasizes how economic choices generate information, while rational-inattention models study the costs of obtaining or processing it ( Bolton and Harris, 1999 ; Sims, 2003 ; Veldkamp, 2011 ) . Contracts with endogenous information examine how informational choices and incentives interact ( Szalay, 2009 ) . Meng et al. (2022) analyze dynamic mechanism design with evolving private information and network interactions. In a more general setting, Tian (2026b) develop a theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly accommodates endogenous information acquisition, production, learning, use, and disclosure together with hidden actions. Related working papers examine informational evolution and joint information–incentive design, and dynamic mechanisms in AI-agent environments ( Tian, 2026c ; Tian, 2026a ) ; see also Pavan et al. (2014) and Ball (2023) for dynamic mechanism design and information provision. The present paper isolates a distinct static auction problem: a seller chooses the initial disclosure experiment, bidders subsequently choose costly private verification, and the seller anticipates the resulting Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium. The analysis characterizes disclosure–verification nonseparability without invoking the additional restrictions of dynamic contracting. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the environment and information technology. Section 3 analyzes equilibrium verification and the seller’s disclosure problem. Section 4 establishes the failure of the benchmark disclosure conclusion in uniform and binary valuation environments. Section 5 develops the revenue decomposition, global implementability and optimality characterization, and disclosure–verification nonseparability. Section 6 develops tractable necessary conditions, restricted structural results, and comparative statics. The proof of the uniform three-bidder comparison uses Sturm’s theorem and exact rational bounds directly in Section 4.

sections.heading: 2 Economic Environment and Information Technology
sections.text: We begin with the independent private-value auction environment of Bergemann et al. (2022), retaining their basic assumptions and notation to facilitate comparison. The seller chooses how much information bidders receive about their own valuations before the auction. We extend this environment by allowing bidders to acquire additional information through costly, privately chosen verification. New notation is introduced only for this additional information-acquisition technology and its outcomes.

sections.heading: 2.3 Timing and the Classical Benchmark
sections.text: The sequence of decisions is as follows. First, the seller publicly commits to a symmetric private information structure. Valuations v i v_{i} are independently drawn from F F , and the seller’s information structure generates a private signal s i s_{i} for each bidder. Second, after observing her signal, each bidder simultaneously chooses a privately observed verification effort e i e_{i} and incurs the corresponding cost. Third, the information-production technology Y i Y_{i} generates the additional private observation z i z_{i} , and each bidder updates her expected valuation to w i p w_{i}^{p} . Finally, bidders submit their bids, and the object and payments are determined by the second-price auction. We consider symmetric Bayesian verification equilibria. Each bidder chooses her verification effort to maximize expected auction payoff net of verification cost, taking the verification strategies of other bidders as given. The seller chooses the initial information structure to maximize expected revenue, anticipating the resulting symmetric verification equilibrium. Our equilibrium analysis concerns symmetric strategies and does not presume uniqueness among arbitrary asymmetric equilibria. The classical model is recovered when additional verification is unavailable. In that case, G p = G G^{p}=G , and the seller chooses a feasible distribution of posterior expected valuations to maximize the expected second-highest bid. Bergemann et al. (2022) establish that an optimal symmetric disclosure policy fully reveals values below a cutoff and pools values above it: valuations below a critical quantile q N ∗ q_{N}^{*} are fully revealed, while valuations above that quantile are pooled at their conditional expectation. The critical quantile depends on the number of bidders but not on the underlying distribution F F . For three bidders with independent uniform valuations on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , q 3 ∗ = 1 / 4 q_{3}^{*}=1/4 , and the optimal expected revenue is 283 / 512 283/512 , compared with 1 / 2 1/2 under full disclosure. With endogenous verification, the seller retains the same choice of initial information structures, but must evaluate each policy at the verification equilibrium it induces. The seller’s problem is therefore to choose a Bayes-plausible distribution of posterior beliefs that maximizes R N ​ ( G p ) R_{N}(G^{p}) , subject to bidders’ equilibrium verification decisions. This formulation preserves the classical auction environment while incorporating bidders’ privately chosen information acquisition.

sections.heading: 3 Verification Equilibrium and the Seller’s Disclosure Problem
sections.text: The seller’s disclosure policy determines the information initially available to bidders, but their final information also depends on privately chosen verification efforts. To evaluate any disclosure policy, we must first determine these efforts in equilibrium. The central difficulty is that a bidder’s benefit from verification depends on competing bids, whose distribution is itself affected by other bidders’ verification decisions. We characterize this interaction by first deriving the value of verification, then establishing the existence and uniqueness of symmetric verification equilibrium, and then formulating the seller’s disclosure problem. For the theoretical analysis that follows, we assume that the valuation space is a compact interval V = [ 0 , M ] V=[0,M] , where M < ∞ M<\infty . This additional regularity condition ensures that the relevant spaces of probability measures are compact under weak convergence. We retain the strictly convex common verification cost c c introduced in Section 2, imposing additional differentiability only where needed.

sections.heading: 5 Revenue Decomposition and General Optimality
sections.text: Section 3 establishes the symmetric verification equilibrium for an arbitrary Bayes-plausible experiment, and Section 4 shows that the familiar benchmark pattern of revealing lower valuations and pooling higher valuations need not remain optimal when verification is endogenous. The purpose of this section is to develop the general theory behind that finding. We first decompose seller revenue into information and verification-related components. We then characterize the final-bid distributions that can arise in verification equilibrium and state exact necessary and sufficient conditions for global optimality. Finally, we identify the cross-signal incentive interaction that makes disclosure and verification inseparable in general. The three parts are complementary: revenue decomposition identifies the objective, implementability restricts the attainable outcomes, and incentive interaction explains why those restrictions respond to the seller’s disclosure choice. The argument draws on the information-design formulation of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022) while keeping endogenous acquisition incentives explicit. Unlike the general dynamic screening framework, the auction studied here is static; the relevant interaction is captured by the equilibrium verification system rather than intertemporal incentive constraints.

sections.heading: 6 Tractable Optimality Conditions and Comparative Statics
sections.text: The general results of Section 5 establish what it means for a bid distribution to be equilibrium implementable and globally revenue maximizing. Their unrestricted formulation, however, need not yield an explicit optimal disclosure policy, even for simple valuation distributions. We therefore turn to the operational consequences of the characterization: necessary conditions from feasible changes in disclosure; posterior contact and extreme-point methods that simplify auxiliary problems; exact structural reductions within specified policy classes; and comparative statics of the resulting conditions. The aim is not a universal closed-form solution or an unrestricted finite-support theorem. Rather, the goal is to formulate correct restrictions that candidate policies must satisfy and exploit their violation to exclude policies from global optimality. The convex-order approach in Bergemann et al. (2022) and the extreme-point geometry of Kleiner, Moldovanu, and Strack (2021) and Kleiner, Moldovanu, Strack, and Whitmeyer (2026) motivate these reductions. Because verification is endogenous, an extreme-point property of a fixed- H H auxiliary problem does not by itself establish an extreme-point optimum for the seller. We distinguish exact identities, conditional structural restrictions, and research extensions accordingly.

sections.heading: 6.1 Equilibrium-Adjusted Necessary Conditions and Posterior Reductions
sections.text: The exact global characterization in Subsection 5.2 does not presuppose finitely many posterior signals, yet direct maximization over all experiments remains demanding. Extreme-point and contact-set methods provide a disciplined route to simplification. In the classical problem, convex order and the geometry of mean-preserving contractions can make extreme experiments particularly useful. Kleiner, Moldovanu, and Strack (2021) characterize extreme points under majorization restrictions, while Kleiner, Moldovanu, Strack, and Whitmeyer (2026) study extreme mean-preserving contractions and the geometry of their finite supports. Here the additional verification-equilibrium fixed point changes the seller’s objective, so a reduction valid for a linearized fixed-distribution auxiliary problem must not be silently promoted to an unrestricted finite-signal representation. For fixed G p G^{p} and g g , Proposition 5.5 is already an exact support restriction whenever a minimizing posterior price exists. In particular, a finite contact set reduces the corresponding auxiliary problem to finitely many posterior weights. This does not yet prove that the seller’s globally optimal disclosure can be selected from that contact set, because the equilibrium bid distribution must be recomputed when the experiment changes. We therefore separate conditional algebraic reductions from general necessary optimality tests.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper revisits optimal information disclosure in auctions through the familiar principle of “trust, but verify.” The fundamental insight is that information disclosure determines not only what bidders learn from the seller, but also what they have incentives to learn on their own. This creates two interrelated trade-offs. The seller must balance the direct effects of disclosure on competition and information rents against its indirect effects on bidders’ incentives to acquire information privately. Each bidder, in turn, must weigh the benefits of more accurate information against the costs of verification, taking into account the information-acquisition decisions of competing bidders. These trade-offs interact through equilibrium: withholding information may preserve the seller’s informational advantage, but it may also induce bidders to reduce that advantage through private verification. The seller controls initial disclosure, but not the information ultimately acquired by bidders. In the spirit of Hurwicz’s incentive-based perspective and the structural-invariance concern highlighted by the Lucas critique, the policy-induced verification response cannot be treated as fixed when disclosure changes. This fundamental tension explains why the distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann et al. (2022)—revealing low values while pooling high values at a critical quantile determined solely by the number of bidders—is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once private verification is endogenous. Thus, the robustness of the benchmark policy across valuation distributions does not extend generally to an environment in which bidders can respond to disclosure by acquiring information for themselves. Recognizing the limitations of the benchmark policy leads to a more general question: how should a seller design information disclosure when bidders’ subsequent information acquisition is determined endogenously in equilibrium? To address this question, we develop a framework that connects bidders’ Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium with the seller’s optimal information design problem. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric verification equilibrium and the existence of an optimal disclosure policy, characterize equilibrium implementability, and derive an exact revenue decomposition that identifies the competing effects of disclosure and verification. Building on these results, we provide a general characterization of global optimality, together with tractable necessary conditions, structural reductions, and comparative-static results under the relevant conditions. The resulting analysis shows why optimal disclosure cannot generally be determined by treating information acquisition as fixed or by optimizing the final distribution of bidders’ information independently of the incentives that generate it. The relevant object of design is the interaction between the seller’s information policy and the equilibrium information-acquisition decisions it induces. The economic mechanism extends beyond the particular auction environment studied here. Reserve prices and alternative auction formats, including uniform-price auctions, introduce additional margins through which disclosure may influence private verification and seller revenue. Similarly, allowing costly participation and private verification to be jointly endogenous would connect information acquisition with bidders’ entry decisions. Establishing optimal disclosure in these environments requires further analysis of the corresponding equilibria. Nevertheless, the central lesson is more general: when agents can privately produce information in response to what is publicly disclosed, information design and information acquisition become inseparable parts of the same economic problem. Optimal disclosure must therefore account not only for the information the designer provides, but also for the information that agents are induced to acquire for themselves.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.38263v1 [econ.TH] 28 Oct 2026 Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification Guoqiang Tian First draft: July 2026; Revised: October 27, 2026 Abstract We revisit the influential distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022), whose optimal disclosure policy reveals low bidder values and pools high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders, and show that this policy is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once bidders can endogenously acquire private information through costly verification. The underlying reason reflects a fundamental principle of incentive-based mechanism design, rooted in Hurwicz’s analysis of structural invariance and echoed in the Lucas critique: economic agents respond strategically to changes in the information and incentives they face. This is the essence of trust, but verify . A change in disclosure policy may leave the underlying economic primitives unchanged while altering bidders’ verification decisions and the resulting equilibrium information structure. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium, characterize equilibrium-implementable disclosure policies, and derive an exact revenue decomposition and a general characterization of global optimality. We further develop optimality conditions and structural results that provide a systematic foundation for analyzing optimal disclosure with endogenous information acquisition. Keywords: optimal information disclosure; endogenous information acquisition; costly verification; impossibility result; disclosure–verification trade-offs; classic auctions. JEL classifications: D44, D82, D83. 1 Introduction How much information should a seller disclose to bidders in an auction? Providing more information can help bidders determine what an object is worth to them and improve the allocation of the object. But better-informed bidders may also obtain greater information rents, reducing the seller’s revenue. Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022, henceforth BHMSW) study this trade-off in a classic second-price auction in which bidders initially do not know their own valuations and the seller chooses what information they receive. They establish a striking result: the revenue-maximizing disclosure policy fully reveals low values while pooling high values. Under this low-value-revelation/high-value-pooling policy, the cutoff is determined by the number of bidders in quantile space, independently of the underlying distribution of valuations. Although developed for second-price auctions, BHMSW explain that their benchmark result also applies to classical revenue-equivalent auction formats, including first-price and all-pay auctions, under the relevant independent private-value assumptions. The strength of this result lies in its simple disclosure structure and distribution-independent critical quantile. It is therefore natural to ask whether the same policy remains optimal when the bidders themselves can respond to the seller’s disclosure by producing information. This is not a change in the auction’s allocation rule or in the prior distribution of values. It is a change in what bidders can do after receiving the information the seller chooses to provide. As we show, that additional margin is enough to overturn the generality of the benchmark disclosure conclusion. In many auctions, however, bidders do not rely exclusively on information supplied by the seller. Consider auctions of valuable artworks, antiques, and other collectibles. Sellers provide descriptions and information about the objects offered for sale, but prospective buyers may also conduct their own investigations to determine what those objects are worth to them. Such behavior follows a familiar principle: trust, but verify. Even when the seller’s information is reliable, it need not be sufficient for a bidder to assess her own valuation. Further investigation can provide valuable information, but requires time, effort, or money. The bidder must decide whether obtaining that information is worth its cost. For a buyer considering a painting or an antique, the question is not simply whether to believe a catalogue entry. Information can be credible and still incomplete for deciding how much to bid. A buyer may examine provenance records, commission an independent appraisal, inspect the object, or seek evidence about authenticity and condition. Doing so takes resources; choosing not to do so leaves the buyer exposed to uncertainty. The familiar injunction to “trust, but verify” therefore has a direct strategic meaning in an auction: what a bidder learns privately depends on the information already disclosed, the cost of further investigation, and the bids she expects to face. This possibility changes the seller’s disclosure problem. Pooling high values may increase revenue by limiting the information rents bidders obtain from the seller’s disclosure. Yet the uncertainty left by pooling can also encourage bidders to acquire additional information privately. The seller therefore faces two related considerations: how disclosure directly affects competition and revenue, and how it changes bidders’ incentives to verify their values. Each bidder faces a corresponding trade-off between the expected benefit of making a better-informed bidding decision and the cost of verification. Moreover, the value of verification depends on how well informed competing bidders are. The seller’s disclosure policy and bidders’ information-acquisition decisions are consequently linked through equilibrium behavior. The principle of “trust, but verify” reflects a deeper lesson of incentive-based economic analysis: agents do not passively accept the information supplied by a designer, but respond to the incentives created by the designer’s policy. This observation echoes Hurwicz (1962) ’s fundamental insight that structural relationships must be understood relative to the changes under consideration, and the related concern underlying the Lucas (1976) critique that policy changes may alter agents’ behavioral decision rules. In the present setting, a change in disclosure policy leaves the underlying valuation environment and verification technology unchanged, but changes bidders’ incentives to acquire information and hence the equilibrium informational environment in which the auction operates. The seller cannot therefore evaluate alternative disclosure policies while treating bidders’ information-acquisition decisions as invariant. Information disclosure is not merely a choice of what information to reveal; it is also an intervention that changes the incentives to learn. This interaction has a central implication. The distribution-independent optimal disclosure result established by Bergemann et al. (2022)—revealing low values while pooling high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders—does not remain generally revenue maximizing when verification is an endogenous choice. We establish the failure of that recommendation in two of the most elementary and familiar valuation environments in auction theory: uniform and binary values. The significance of these findings is not that a specially tailored distribution creates an exception. Rather, the benchmark policy already loses its generality in settings that normally serve as the starting point for auction analysis. The original BHMSW theorem remains valid under its own assumptions; what does not survive is the extension of its optimal disclosure conclusion to a world in which bidders can privately verify their values. The economic reason is the seller’s interaction with bidders’ information production. Revealing information can improve bidding decisions while raising information rents; withholding it may limit those rents while inducing bidders to learn for themselves. A bidder, in turn, weighs the expected advantage of better information against the cost of verification, taking into account how informed her competitors are likely to become. Thus neither the seller’s disclosure choice nor a bidder’s verification choice can be assessed in isolation. The relevant object is the Bayesian Nash equilibrium induced by each disclosure policy, and the seller compares revenues across those equilibria. We study this interaction by extending the independent private-value environment of BHMSW. The seller continues to choose symmetric, independent private information experiments about bidders’ original valuations, and the object is sold through a second-price auction. After receiving the seller’s signal, however, each bidder may privately undertake costly verification to learn more about her own valuation. Verification is a hidden action, and its outcome provides additional private information without changing the underlying valuation. We focus on a simple information-production technology in which the bidder chooses an effort that determines the probability of learning her valuation perfectly. The seller anticipates the equilibrium verification decisions when choosing the initial information structure. The distinction between information disclosed by the seller and information acquired by bidders is important. In the original disclosure problem, the seller can choose the distribution of bidders’ posterior expected valuations, subject to Bayes plausibility. Once verification is possible, the same distribution of posterior means may induce different information-acquisition incentives. A bidder’s willingness to verify depends not only on her expected valuation but also on the uncertainty that remains about her actual value. Thus, the seller must take account of the full posterior beliefs generated by disclosure and the subsequent information choices of bidders. The failure of the benchmark policy also creates a constructive problem: if the seller cannot treat the final information in bidders’ hands as something she directly controls, how should optimal disclosure be characterized? Our analysis proceeds from the bidders’ Bayesian Nash equilibrium in private verification to the seller’s feasible equilibrium outcomes, and then to general revenue and optimality conditions. This positive theory complements the main economic finding rather than merely providing a way to calculate the examples. Our first contribution, developed in Section 3, is to characterize the equilibrium of this information-acquisition game. A bidder’s gain from verification depends on the distribution of competing bids, which in turn depends on their verification decisions. This strategic feedback leads to a fixed-point problem that must be resolved before evaluating the seller’s disclosure policy. We show that the symmetric verification equilibrium admits a convex-potential representation, which establishes existence and uniqueness under strictly convex verification costs. The associated equilibrium Jacobian has a positive-semidefinite Gram structure, providing a tractable characterization of equilibrium interactions and comparative statics. We extend the existence and uniqueness results from finite signal structures to arbitrary posterior distributions using fixed-point and potential arguments. The resulting equilibrium characterization also establishes continuity of the final-bid distribution with respect to the seller’s information experiment, a key step in proving the existence of an optimal disclosure policy over the unrestricted experiment space. Our second contribution, developed in Section 5, concerns optimal disclosure for general distributions of bidder values. We characterize which final-bid distributions can arise from a Bayes-plausible private disclosure experiment together with the bidders’ equilibrium verification choices. The characterization applies to the unrestricted space of private information experiments rather than a prespecified family of disclosure policies. Using convex separation and concavification, we obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for equilibrium implementability, together with a posterior-price dual representation. These results provide an infinite-dimensional characterization of feasible disclosure outcomes without requiring concavity of the seller’s revenue function or imposing a particular form on the optimal experiment. This general characterization addresses a difficulty created by endogenous information acquisition. Although the seller chooses the initial information structure, she does not directly choose the final distribution of bids. That distribution results from the combination of disclosure and bidders’ privately chosen verification efforts. Consequently, standard information-design arguments based only on distributions of posterior means are no longer sufficient. Our characterization identifies the additional equilibrium restrictions that a final-bid distribution must satisfy. It provides a general description of feasible disclosure outcomes without imposing a particular structure on the seller’s optimal experiment. In Sections 5 and 6, to study the structure of optimal disclosure more directly, we derive the revenue effects of changes in the seller’s information policy, allowing verification efforts to adjust in equilibrium. Using the implicit-function theorem, we separate the direct effect of disclosure on bidding from the indirect effect operating through endogenous verification. We also develop a rare-signal splitting test that introduces new private signals while preserving Bayes plausibility. The resulting directional condition accounts for both equilibrium effort adjustments and changes in the distribution of bids, including moving bid atoms. This provides a rigorous test of whether a proposed disclosure policy can be improved and plays a central role in establishing the failure of the benchmark disclosure structure. Our third contribution, established in Section 4, is a sharp result on that question. We first characterize verification equilibrium under the benchmark policy for general distributions of bidder values. In this case, bidders whose values are fully revealed have no reason to verify, while those receiving the pooled high-value signal face a nontrivial information-acquisition decision. The equilibrium therefore reduces to a one-dimensional problem. For three bidders with uniformly distributed valuations, we obtain closed-form expressions for verification effort and seller revenue, allowing us to study how endogenous verification changes the optimal pooling cutoff. The analysis in Section 4 shows that the benchmark disclosure conclusion of BHMSW does not generally survive endogenous information acquisition. Consider three bidders with independent uniform valuations and quadratic verification costs. We first identify the revenue-maximizing policy within the entire class of policies that reveal lower values and pool higher values. We then construct an admissible refinement of its high-value pool and account for the verification equilibrium induced by the refined information structure. The refinement yields strictly higher expected revenue than the optimal policy within that benchmark class. The comparison is established analytically by an exact polynomial root count and rational revenue bounds, rather than inferred from a numerical comparison of selected disclosure policies. The economic mechanism behind this result is the interaction between pooling and private verification. Pooling high values can benefit the seller when bidders do not acquire additional information. But the same pooling leaves uncertainty that bidders may find worthwhile to resolve. Refining the high-value pool changes not only what bidders initially know but also how much additional information they choose to acquire. The seller can therefore gain from a disclosure policy that would not be optimal if bidders’ information-acquisition decisions were held fixed. The failure of low-value revelation and high-value pooling arises from this equilibrium response, not from any change in the auction format or in bidders’ original valuation distributions. Our findings distinguish the value of partial disclosure from the particular structure of optimal partial disclosure. The result of BHMSW remains valid in their original environment, which is recovered when additional information acquisition is unavailable. In our extended environment, full disclosure need not be optimal either. What changes is the revenue-maximizing way of withholding and revealing information. The counterexample establishes that no policy in that benchmark class is optimal in the specified environment, although it does not identify an explicit optimal experiment over the unrestricted disclosure space. The general equilibrium and implementability results provide a framework for studying that broader problem. Our analysis relates to two strands of research. The first studies information disclosure and Bayesian persuasion, where a designer chooses an information structure to influence subsequent decisions. BHMSW apply this approach to classic auctions and establish the benchmark result that serves as our point of departure. The second studies endogenous information acquisition, including bidders’ incentives to learn before participating in auctions. Our contribution connects these approaches: the seller chooses an information structure while anticipating that bidders will respond by privately acquiring additional information. This interaction changes both the set of equilibrium bidding outcomes and the structure of the seller’s optimal disclosure policy. Related Literature Our study draws most directly on two lines of research: the design of information disclosed by an auction seller and the costly acquisition of information by bidders. Bergemann et al. (2022) provide the central benchmark by identifying a revenue-maximizing rule that reveals lower values and pools higher values in a second-price auction. Their analysis highlights the tension between the allocative gains from informing bidders and the information rents that more precise private knowledge may create. Our question is what happens to that conclusion when the seller’s disclosure also changes bidders’ incentives to learn privately. The auction format and the distribution of underlying valuations are unchanged; the new margin is the endogenous information acquired after the seller’s signals. The two familiar valuation environments examined in Section 4 show why that margin matters for the robustness of the benchmark conclusion ( Bergemann et al., 2022 ) . The classical auction literature emphasizes the role of information in bidding and revenue. Milgrom and Weber (1982a) develop the foundational analysis of auctions with interdependent information and the consequences of information disclosure; Milgrom and Weber (1982b) study the value and strategic acquisition of information in sealed-bid auctions. Bergemann and Pesendorfer (2007) analyze the joint choice of an optimal auction and bidders’ information structures. These approaches provide essential antecedents for studying information as an economic design margin. Our question is narrower in auction format but different in equilibrium timing: the second-price auction is fixed, and seller disclosure precedes bidders’ privately chosen costly verification ( Milgrom and Weber, 1982a ; Milgrom and Weber, 1982b ; Bergemann and Pesendorfer, 2007 ) . A closely related literature studies strategic and costly information acquisition in auctions. Persico (2000) examines the incentives to acquire information under alternative auction mechanisms; Bobkova (2024) studies how auction formats shape the information about an object that bidders choose to learn. These contributions show why an information-acquisition decision is itself part of auction behavior rather than an exogenous input to bidding. We instead hold the second-price auction fixed and allow the seller to choose what bidders initially learn before their costly private verification decisions. This distinction is important: the verification decisions form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium and change the final distribution of bids through which the seller’s disclosure affects revenue ( Persico, 2000 ; Bobkova, 2024 ) . A further auction-theoretic connection concerns endogenous costly decisions before bidding. Bergemann and Välimäki (2002) study incentives for private information acquisition under mechanism design. In an earlier line of research, Cao and Tian (2010) analyze equilibrium participation decisions in first- and second-price auctions with participation costs; Cao et al. (2018) study related second-price environments, including privately known participation costs. These studies already feature the central economic insight that bidders compare the expected equilibrium benefit of a privately costly choice with its cost, taking other bidders’ choices into account. In the present paper, the costly choice concerns verification rather than entry, and the new design margin is the seller’s information disclosure, which endogenously changes the benefit of acquiring private information ( Bergemann and Välimäki, 2002 ; Cao and Tian, 2010 ; Cao et al., 2018 ) . Our approach also connects to the broader literature on statistical experiments and information design. Blackwell’s comparison of experiments provides a foundational language for informativeness; Bayesian persuasion and Bayes-correlated-equilibrium approaches emphasize the choice of informational structures and the resulting constraints on beliefs and behavior ( Blackwell, 1953 ; Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011 ; Bergemann and Morris, 2016 ; Bergemann and Morris, 2019 ) . Bergemann, Bonatti, and Smolin (2018) study information as an economic object that can itself be designed and priced. Joint mechanism–information design similarly underscores the importance of coordinating informational and incentive instruments ( Bergemann et al., 2018 ; Bergemann et al., 2026a ) . In the present setting, however, the seller does not directly choose the final information on which bids are based. Initial posterior beliefs determine verification incentives, and the equilibrium information acquired by bidders determines the eventual bidding distribution. Section 5 characterizes precisely this additional implementability restriction. The distinction between supplying information and inducing private learning also arises outside auctions. Crémer and Khalil (1992), Lewis and Sappington (1994), and Crémer, Khalil, and Rochet (1998) examine how contractual and informational arrangements affect incentives to become informed. These studies help distinguish information already held by agents from information they choose to acquire after observing an institutional decision. The present paper carries this interaction into a seller’s optimal disclosure problem with competing bidders and equilibrium verification ( Crémer and Khalil, 1992 ; Lewis and Sappington, 1994 ; Crémer et al., 1998 ) . A further connection is to endogenous information production and dynamic mechanism design. Research on experimentation emphasizes how economic choices generate information, while rational-inattention models study the costs of obtaining or processing it ( Bolton and Harris, 1999 ; Sims, 2003 ; Veldkamp, 2011 ) . Contracts with endogenous information examine how informational choices and incentives interact ( Szalay, 2009 ) . Meng et al. (2022) analyze dynamic mechanism design with evolving private information and network interactions. In a more general setting, Tian (2026b) develop a theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly accommodates endogenous information acquisition, production, learning, use, and disclosure together with hidden actions. Related working papers examine informational evolution and joint information–incentive design, and dynamic mechanisms in AI-agent environments ( Tian, 2026c ; Tian, 2026a ) ; see also Pavan et al. (2014) and Ball (2023) for dynamic mechanism design and information provision. The present paper isolates a distinct static auction problem: a seller chooses the initial disclosure experiment, bidders subsequently choose costly private verification, and the seller anticipates the resulting Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium. The analysis characterizes disclosure–verification nonseparability without invoking the additional restrictions of dynamic contracting. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the environment and information technology. Section 3 analyzes equilibrium verification and the seller’s disclosure problem. Section 4 establishes the failure of the benchmark disclosure conclusion in uniform and binary valuation environments. Section 5 develops the revenue decomposition, global implementability and optimality characterization, and disclosure–verification nonseparability. Section 6 develops tractable necessary conditions, restricted structural results, and comparative statics. The proof of the uniform three-bidder comparison uses Sturm’s theorem and exact rational bounds directly in Section 4. 2 Economic Environment and Information Technology We begin with the independent private-value auction environment of Bergemann et al. The information order provides necessary restrictions on the distributions induced by disclosure and verification, but it does not by itself characterize equilibrium outcomes. A bidder’s verification effort must also be optimal given the distribution of competing bids. Verification can improve her bidding decision, but she must weigh the expected benefit against its cost. Since competing bids depend on competitors’ verification choices, the value of verification itself depends on the equilibrium information-acquisition decisions of other bidders. The resulting final-bid distribution must therefore satisfy both Bayesian information feasibility and bidders’ verification incentives. The classical analysis of bidding under information asymmetries provides the auction-theoretic starting point for this environment ( Milgrom and Weber, 1982a ; Milgrom and Weber, 1982b ) .
